# City × industry heat checklists that pair with digital WBGT.

> Ten live heat illness prevention guides — Phoenix construction, Houston roofing, Las Vegas landscaping, California construction, Dallas utilities, Miami delivery, Tucson agriculture, and Atlanta film & events, San Antonio oil & gas, and Orlando landscaping — paired with GOES digital WBGT and live heat-risk scores.

HTML version: https://heatready.goes.health/

Checklists + digital WBGT for hot jobsites



HeatReady Guides publishes practical heat illness prevention pages for construction,
roofing, landscaping, utilities, agriculture, and delivery crews — then points you to
**GOES digital WBGT** (wet-bulb globe temperature) and live heat-risk scores
so crews act on more than air temperature alone. Print the checklist. Watch the score.
Keep people safer.

- [Browse all ten guides](https://heatready.goes.health/guides/index.html)
- [Phoenix Construction](https://heatready.goes.health/guides/phoenix-construction.md)
- [California Construction](https://heatready.goes.health/guides/california-construction-3395.md)
- [Digital WBGT & live heat-risk scores](https://goes.health/?utm_source=llms_txt&utm_medium=agent&utm_campaign=heatready)

## Why this exists

Weather apps say “103°F.” Crews need “15-minute cool-down every 45 minutes, hydrate
8–12 oz every 15–20 minutes, shade up, buddy check” — and a heat score that reflects
humidity, sun, and radiant load, not air temp alone. We publish the checklist; GOES
delivers digital WBGT and live heat-risk scores.

### By city

Phoenix, Houston, Las Vegas, California, Dallas, Miami, Tucson, Atlanta, San Antonio, Orlando — climate and local context that matter on the ground.

### By industry

Construction, roofing, landscaping, utilities, agriculture, delivery — different PPE, work rates, and shade options.

### Printable & plain

Checklists, trigger tables, emergency steps. Mobile-first. Works without JavaScript. Print-friendly.

### Why WBGT beats air temp

Wet-bulb globe temperature folds in humidity, radiant heat (sun / steel / asphalt),
and air movement — closer to what outdoor crews feel than a dry-bulb “103°F” alone.
Use HeatReady triggers with GOES digital WBGT when conditions climb.

### Digital WBGT from GOES

Pair each guide with [GOES](https://goes.health/?utm_source=llms_txt&utm_medium=agent&utm_campaign=heatready) digital WBGT and live
heat-risk scores so supervisors can escalate water–rest–shade from a live signal,
not just the airport forecast.

### Plan + live score

Static checklists set the program. Digital WBGT tells you when today’s worksite
crossed into the next control band — see the [GOES platform](https://goes.health/platform?utm_source=llms_txt&utm_medium=agent&utm_campaign=heatready).

**Not legal advice.** HeatReady Guides summarize common best practices aligned with
publicly available OSHA / NIOSH heat guidance and general state/local awareness. Your obligations
depend on federal, state, and local rules for your worksite. Confirm with your safety counsel or
compliance team.

# Phoenix Construction Heat Illness Prevention Checklist

> Printable Phoenix construction heat checklist paired with GOES digital WBGT and live heat-risk scores: water, shade, rest, triggers. Not legal advice.

HTML version: https://heatready.goes.health/guides/phoenix-construction.html

A supervisor-ready checklist for outdoor construction crews in the Phoenix metro — water, shade, rest, acclimatization, buddy checks, and emergency steps. Brief the crew
before a hot shift; pair checklist triggers with
**GOES digital WBGT** (wet-bulb globe temperature) and live heat-risk scores
when conditions climb.

- [Get live Phoenix WBGT / heat-risk scores](https://goes.health/?utm_source=llms_txt&utm_medium=agent&utm_campaign=heatready)

**Not legal advice.** This page summarizes common heat-illness prevention practices
aligned with publicly available OSHA / NIOSH-style guidance and general Arizona / Phoenix
heat awareness. It is not a substitute for your written heat plan, training records, or
counsel. Confirm requirements for your contracts and jurisdiction.

## Phoenix summer risk — what crews actually feel

Phoenix sits in the Sonoran Desert. From June through September, daytime highs commonly
reach the upper 90s to well above 100°F. National Weather Service climate normals for
Phoenix (Sky Harbor area) put average July daily highs near **106°F**, with
June and August also frequently above 100°F. Overnight lows often stay in the 80s, so
recovery between shifts can be limited.

The North American monsoon (roughly July–September) can raise humidity and dew points.
That makes the same air temperature feel harder on the body — heat index and perceived
strain climb even when the dry-bulb reading looks “familiar.” Pair temperature checks
with humidity / heat-index awareness on monsoon afternoons.

Climate context based on publicly available NWS / NOAA Phoenix climate normals and
monsoon-season humidity patterns. Always check the day’s forecast and worksite readings.

- ~106°: Typical July avg high (Phoenix)
- 100°+: Common Jun–Sep afternoon highs
- Monsoon: Higher humidity Jul–Sep

## Jobsite checklist

Check these before the shift and again when the heat climbs. Print this section for the gang box.

- **Water** — Cool potable water close to the work area. Aim for enough for about 1 quart (32 oz) per worker per hour, or a reliable top-up system. Encourage small sips every 15–20 minutes — not chugging only at lunch.
- **Shade / cool-down area** — Pop-up canopies, trailers, or building shade ready before high heat. Enough space for cool-down rests without crowding. Anyone can request a preventative cool-down rest; do not send symptomatic workers back until recovered.
- **Rest & work–rest cycles** — Schedule breaks that increase as heat index rises. Prefer earlier starts and heavier tasks in cooler hours. Reduce pace / rotate jobs on extreme days.
- **Acclimatization** — New hires, temps, and anyone returning from leave need a gradual ramp (often ~1–2 weeks of increasing heat exposure). Watch them more closely the first days on a hot Phoenix site.
- **Buddy system** — Pair workers to watch for confusion, stumbling, heavy sweating or sudden stop of sweating, nausea, headache, or irritability. Supervisors check in on high-heat days — especially lone tasks.
- **Emergency readiness** — Know who calls 911, cell coverage gaps, gate codes / cross streets for EMS, nearest ER, and cooling first aid (shade, loosen PPE if safe, cool with water). Never leave a symptomatic worker alone or send them home without evaluating care needs.
- **Training & language** — Pre-shift huddle: today’s triggers, water locations, stop-work authority, symptom reporting. Deliver in languages the crew understands.

## Heat index / high-heat trigger table

Example outdoor-construction triggers aligned with common OSHA / NIOSH heat-awareness practice
(water–rest–shade, increasing controls as heat rises). Adjust to your written plan, PPE load,
and radiant heat on steel / roof decks. Where your program uses WBGT or heat-index bands,
escalate the same controls when GOES digital WBGT / live heat-risk scores move into the next
band — not only when the airport dry-bulb hits a round number.
**Not a regulatory substitute.**

| Heat index (approx.) | Risk band | Suggested controls |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 80–90°F | Caution | Water available; encourage hydration; shade on request; watch new workers. |
| 91–103°F | High | Shade up; scheduled cool-down breaks; remind water every 15–20 min; buddy checks. |
| 103–115°F | Very high | Shorten work cycles; more frequent rests; supervisor observation; delay non-essential heavy tasks. |
| Above ~115°F | Extreme | Maximum controls or stop outdoor work where feasible; prioritize cooling and EMS readiness. |

Heat-index bands mirror widely published NIOSH / OSHA heat-awareness charts used for outdoor work planning.
Measure conditions at the worksite; rooftop and unshaded concrete run hotter than the airport reading.
Wet-bulb globe temperature (WBGT) accounts for humidity, radiant heat, and air movement — pair these
checklist triggers with [GOES digital WBGT](https://goes.health/?utm_source=llms_txt&utm_medium=agent&utm_campaign=heatready) when you need a live score.

## Local / regulatory note (high level)

Arizona employers remain subject to federal OSHA (ADOSH) expectations under the General Duty
Clause for recognized heat hazards, plus any contract-specific rules. The City of Phoenix has
advanced contractor-focused heat safety expectations for covered City work (written heat plans,
water, rest, shade / cooling, training, documentation). Statewide heat-safety guidelines have
also been under active development — treat heat as a documented program, not informal advice.

If you bid or perform Phoenix municipal work, confirm whether the City worker heat-safety
ordinance and flow-down clauses apply to you and your subcontractors. Keep the written plan
on site and log what you actually did each hot day.

This is general awareness only — not legal advice and not a compliance guarantee. Verify current
City of Phoenix, ADOSH, and federal OSHA requirements for your jobs.

## Quick answers for Phoenix crews

### How much water should we stage for an 8-hour shift?

A common planning figure is about 1 quart per worker per hour (roughly 2 gallons per person
for 8 hours) if you are not plumbed — or start with less only if you have a reliable top-up
route. Keep it cool and next to the work, not only at the trailer.

### When should we treat the day as “high heat”?

Follow your written plan. Many outdoor programs escalate controls as heat index climbs through
the 90s and into triple digits — and sooner with heavy PPE, roof work, or monsoon humidity.
Check the worksite, not only the airport forecast.

### What are early signs of heat illness we train for?

Headache, dizziness, weakness, nausea, irritability, heavy sweating or a sudden stop in
sweating, muscle cramps, and confusion. Cool the person, rest in shade, hydrate if conscious,
and call EMS for severe or worsening symptoms.

### Does this page make us OSHA-compliant?

No. It is an educational checklist. Compliance depends on applicable rules, an effective written
program, training, and what you actually do on site. Use counsel and your safety lead for
formal plans.

### How does GOES digital WBGT fit with this checklist?

HeatReady Guides help you publish and brief a static plan. GOES adds digital WBGT
(wet-bulb globe temperature) and live heat-risk scores so crews can match checklist
triggers to today’s conditions — see
[goes.health](https://goes.health/?utm_source=llms_txt&utm_medium=agent&utm_campaign=heatready) and
[goes.health/platform](https://goes.health/platform?utm_source=llms_txt&utm_medium=agent&utm_campaign=heatready).

# Houston Roofing Crew Heat Safety Plan

> Printable Houston roofing heat checklist paired with GOES digital WBGT and live heat-risk scores: water on the roof, shade at staging, rest triggers. Not legal advice.

HTML version: https://heatready.goes.health/guides/houston-roofing.html

A supervisor-ready plan for Houston roofing crews — water on the roof and near the ladder,
rest and shade triggers, acclimatization, buddy checks, and emergency steps. Brief the crew
before a hot shift; pair checklist triggers with
**GOES digital WBGT** (wet-bulb globe temperature) and live heat-risk scores
when Gulf humidity and radiant roof-deck heat climb.

- [Get live Houston WBGT / heat-risk scores](https://goes.health/?utm_source=llms_txt&utm_medium=agent&utm_campaign=heatready)

**Not legal advice.** This page summarizes common heat-illness prevention practices
aligned with publicly available OSHA / NIOSH-style guidance and general Texas / Houston
heat awareness. It is not a substitute for your written heat plan, training records, or
counsel. Confirm requirements for your contracts and jurisdiction.

## Houston summer risk — humidity + roof radiant heat

Houston has a humid subtropical climate. From June through September, daytime highs commonly
sit in the mid-90s°F. National Weather Service climate normals for the Houston area put
average July daily highs near **94°F**, with June and August also frequently
in the low-to-mid 90s. Overnight lows often stay in the mid-70s, so recovery between shifts
can feel limited when humidity stays high.

Gulf moisture keeps dew points elevated much of the summer. That pushes heat index — what the body feels — routinely over **100°F** even when the dry-bulb reading
looks “only” mid-90s. On open roof decks, dark shingles and membrane add radiant heat that
airport and phone forecasts miss. Pair heat-index awareness with worksite readings, and
escalate using GOES digital WBGT when humidity and radiant load climb together.

Climate context based on publicly available NWS / NOAA Houston-area climate normals and
Gulf Coast summer humidity / heat-index patterns. Always check the day’s forecast and
worksite readings.

- ~94°: Typical July avg high (Houston)
- 100°+: Common summer heat-index peaks
- Gulf: High humidity Jun–Sep

## Jobsite checklist

Check these before the shift and again when the heat climbs. Print this section for the gang box or staging trailer.

- **Water on roof / near ladder** — Cool potable water staged at staging and reachable from the roof (jug at the ridge or near the ladder — not only in the truck). Aim for enough for about 1 quart (32 oz) per worker per hour, or a reliable top-up system. Encourage small sips every 15–20 minutes — not chugging only at lunch.
- **Shade / cool-down area** — Open roof decks have almost no natural shade. Stage trailers, pop-up canopies, or vehicle shade at ground staging before high heat. Plan cool-down rests off the deck when heat climbs. Anyone can request a preventative cool-down rest; do not send symptomatic workers back until recovered.
- **Rest & work–rest cycles** — Schedule breaks that increase as heat index rises. Prefer earlier starts and heavier tear-off / install in cooler hours. Reduce pace / rotate jobs (ridge vs. eave, tear-off vs. cleanup) on extreme humidity days. Factor radiant heat from dark shingles and membrane — the deck runs hotter than the street.
- **Acclimatization** — New hires, temps, and anyone returning from leave need a gradual ramp (often ~1–2 weeks of increasing heat exposure). Watch them more closely the first days on a hot Houston roof — especially after rain when humidity spikes.
- **Buddy system** — Pair workers to watch for confusion, stumbling, heavy sweating or sudden stop of sweating, nausea, headache, or irritability. Supervisors check in on high-heat days — especially lone roofers, ridge work, and anyone on a separate elevation.
- **Emergency readiness** — Know who calls 911, cell coverage gaps, gate codes / cross streets for EMS, ladder and access path for responders, nearest ER, and cooling first aid (get off the hot deck into shade, loosen PPE / hard hat if safe, cool with water). Never leave a symptomatic worker alone on the roof or send them home without evaluating care needs.
- **Training, PPE & language** — Pre-shift huddle: today’s triggers, water locations, stop-work authority, symptom reporting, radiant heat from dark decks, and hard-hat / PPE heat load. Deliver in languages the crew understands.

## Heat index / high-heat trigger table

Example outdoor-roofing triggers aligned with common OSHA / NIOSH heat-awareness practice
(water–rest–shade, increasing controls as heat rises). Adjust to your written plan, PPE load,
and radiant heat on shingles / membrane. Roof decks often run hotter than the airport reading.
Where your program uses WBGT or heat-index bands, escalate the same controls when GOES
digital WBGT / live heat-risk scores move into the next band — not only when the airport
dry-bulb hits a round number.
**Not a regulatory substitute.**

| Heat index (approx.) | Risk band | Suggested controls |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 80–90°F | Caution | Water available on roof / staging; encourage hydration; shade on request at staging; watch new workers. |
| 91–103°F | High | Canopy / trailer shade up at staging; scheduled cool-down breaks off the deck; remind water every 15–20 min; buddy checks. |
| 103–115°F | Very high | Shorten work cycles; more frequent rests off the hot deck; supervisor observation; delay non-essential heavy tear-off. |
| Above ~115°F | Extreme | Maximum controls or stop outdoor roof work where feasible; prioritize cooling and EMS readiness. |

Heat-index bands mirror widely published NIOSH / OSHA heat-awareness charts used for outdoor work planning.
Measure conditions at the worksite; dark roof decks and unshaded membrane run hotter than the airport reading.

checklist triggers with [GOES digital WBGT](https://goes.health/?utm_source=llms_txt&utm_medium=agent&utm_campaign=heatready) when you need a live score.

## Local / regulatory note (high level)

Texas employers remain subject to federal OSHA expectations under the General Duty Clause
for recognized heat hazards, plus any contract-specific rules. There is no separate statewide
heat-illness standard analogous to Cal/OSHA 3395; treat heat as a documented program — water, rest, shade / cooling, training, and emergency response — not informal advice.

City of Houston and Harris County contractor / public-works expectations can include
heat-safety language in covered contracts (written plans, water access, rest, training,
documentation). If you bid or perform municipal or large commercial work in the Houston
metro, confirm flow-down clauses for you and your subcontractors. Keep the written plan
on site and log what you actually did each hot, humid day.

This is general awareness only — not legal advice and not a compliance guarantee. Verify current
City of Houston, Harris County, and federal OSHA requirements for your jobs.

## Quick answers for Houston roofing crews

### Where should we stage water on a roofing job?

Keep cool water at ground staging and reachable from the roof — a jug near the ladder
or at a safe ridge spot beats water that only lives in the truck. A common planning
figure is about 1 quart per worker per hour. Encourage small sips every 15–20 minutes.

### Why does the roof feel hotter than the forecast?

Dark shingles and membrane radiate heat; open decks have little shade; and Houston’s
Gulf humidity pushes heat index well above the dry-bulb reading. Check conditions at
the worksite — and escalate with GOES digital WBGT — not only the airport forecast.

### What are early signs of heat illness we train for?

Headache, dizziness, weakness, nausea, irritability, heavy sweating or a sudden stop in
sweating, muscle cramps, and confusion. Get the person off the hot deck into shade, rest,
hydrate if conscious, and call EMS for severe or worsening symptoms.

### Does this page make us OSHA-compliant in Texas?

No. It is an educational checklist. Texas employers follow federal OSHA (including the
General Duty Clause for recognized heat hazards) plus any contract rules. Compliance
depends on an effective written program, training, and what you actually do on site.

# Las Vegas Landscaping Heat Illness Prevention Guide

> Printable Las Vegas landscaping heat checklist paired with GOES digital WBGT and live heat-risk scores: early starts, water at each stop, canopy shade, dry-heat triggers. Not legal advice.

HTML version: https://heatready.goes.health/guides/las-vegas-landscaping.html

A supervisor-ready plan for Las Vegas landscaping crews — water at every property stop,
early-start pacing, canopy shade on open desert lots, acclimatization, buddy checks, and
emergency steps. Brief the crew before a hot shift; pair checklist triggers with
**GOES digital WBGT** (wet-bulb globe temperature) and live heat-risk scores
when dry heat, reflected rock and asphalt, or monsoon humidity climb.

- [Get live Las Vegas WBGT / heat-risk scores](https://goes.health/?utm_source=llms_txt&utm_medium=agent&utm_campaign=heatready)

**Not legal advice.** This page summarizes common heat-illness prevention practices
aligned with publicly available OSHA / NIOSH-style guidance and general Nevada / Las Vegas
heat awareness. It is not a substitute for your written heat plan, training records, or
counsel. Confirm requirements for your contracts and jurisdiction.

## Las Vegas summer risk — dry heat + radiant ground

Las Vegas sits in the Mojave Desert. From June through September, daytime highs commonly
reach the upper 90s to well above 100°F. National Weather Service climate normals for the
Las Vegas area put average July daily highs near **104°F**, with June often
near 99°F and August also frequently above 100°F. Overnight lows often stay around
**80°F** in July, so recovery between shifts can be limited — especially
with the valley’s urban heat island.

Desert air is usually very dry, so sweat evaporates quickly. Crews can underestimate how
much fluid they are losing because they do not feel “soaked.” Rock, decomposed granite,
gravel, pavers, stucco, and asphalt all add radiant and conductive heat that the airport
forecast misses. The North American monsoon (roughly July–September) can raise humidity
and dew points on some afternoons, making the same air temperature harder on the body.
Pair temperature checks with worksite readings, and escalate using GOES digital WBGT when
radiant load or humidity climbs.

Climate context based on publicly available NWS / NOAA Las Vegas climate normals
(1991–2020) and Mojave Desert summer humidity / monsoon patterns. Always check the day’s
forecast and worksite readings.

- ~104°: Typical July avg high (Las Vegas)
- 100°+: Common Jun–Sep afternoon highs
- Dry heat: Fast fluid loss; monsoon humidity some afternoons

## Jobsite checklist

Check these before the shift and again when the heat climbs. Print this section for the truck binder or gang box.

- **Water at every stop** — Cool potable water in each truck and staged at the property — not only back at the yard. Landscaping crews bounce between HOA lots, new builds, and commercial sites. Aim for enough for about 1 quart (32 oz) per worker per hour, or a reliable top-up system. Encourage small sips every 15–20 minutes — not chugging only at lunch. Dry heat hides how much you are sweating.
- **Shade / cool-down area** — New desert developments and rock-and-gravel lots often have little mature tree shade. Stage pop-up canopies, trailer shade, or a cooled vehicle before high heat, and re-set shade when the crew moves to the next stop. Anyone can request a preventative cool-down rest; do not send symptomatic workers back until recovered.
- **Rest & work–rest cycles** — Schedule breaks that increase as heat index or WBGT rises. Prefer earlier starts (common 4–6 a.m. in valley landscaping) and heavier mowing, planting, or hardscape in cooler hours. Reduce pace / rotate jobs (sun vs. building shade, mowing vs. irrigation checks) on extreme days. Factor radiant heat from rock, gravel, and asphalt — the ground runs hotter than the street forecast.
- **Acclimatization** — New hires, temps, and anyone returning from leave — or new to Mojave dry heat — need a gradual ramp (often ~1–2 weeks of increasing heat exposure). Watch them more closely the first days on a hot Las Vegas route.
- **Buddy system** — Pair workers to watch for confusion, stumbling, heavy sweating or sudden stop of sweating, nausea, headache, or irritability. Supervisors check in on high-heat days — especially when the crew splits across properties or someone works a remote HOA lot alone.
- **Emergency readiness** — Know who calls 911, cell coverage gaps, gate codes / cross streets for EMS (new subdivisions can be hard to describe), nearest ER, and cooling first aid (shade, loosen PPE if safe, cool with water). Never leave a symptomatic worker alone in a hot truck or send them home without evaluating care needs.
- **Training, PPE & language** — Pre-shift huddle: today’s triggers, water locations, stop-work authority, symptom reporting, dry-heat dehydration, and extra heat load from long sleeves, chemical / pesticide PPE, or backpack sprayers. Deliver in languages the crew understands.

and radiant heat on rock, gravel, and asphalt. Where your program uses WBGT or heat-index bands,

**Not a regulatory substitute.**

| 103–115°F | Very high | Shorten work cycles; more frequent rests off hot rock / asphalt; supervisor observation; delay non-essential heavy mowing or hardscape. |

## Local / regulatory note (high level)

Nevada is a state-plan OSHA state. Nevada OSHA’s heat-illness regulation (R131-24AP) has
been in enforcement since April 29, 2025. Covered employers — generally those with more
than 10 employees who must keep a written safety program — are expected to complete a
job hazard analysis for classifications with substantial heat exposure and, if hazards
are identified, maintain a written plan covering potable water, rest when someone shows
symptoms of heat illness, means of cooling, monitoring of hot conditions, training, and
emergency procedures. Employers of every size still have a duty to protect workers from
recognized heat hazards.

Landscaping routes in the Las Vegas / Clark County metro often split crews across HOA,
municipal, and commercial sites. Confirm any contract or flow-down heat-safety language
for you and your subcontractors. Keep the written plan with the crew (truck binder or
phone) and log what you actually did each hot day.

This is general awareness only — not legal advice and not a compliance guarantee. Verify current
Nevada OSHA, Clark County, and City of Las Vegas requirements for your jobs.

## Quick answers for Las Vegas landscaping crews

### Why does dry heat still dehydrate us so fast?

In the Mojave, sweat evaporates quickly, so you may not feel soaked even while you
lose a lot of fluid. Plan about 1 quart per worker per hour, keep water in every truck
and at the property — not only at the yard — and encourage small sips every 15–20 minutes.

### We already start at 5 a.m. Do we still need afternoon controls?

Early starts help, but many routes still run into peak heat. Keep shade, water, and
longer rest cycles ready after mid-morning, and escalate when GOES digital WBGT or
your worksite reading moves into the next band — not only because the clock says noon.

### What are early signs of heat illness we train for?

Headache, dizziness, weakness, nausea, irritability, heavy sweating or a sudden stop in
sweating, muscle cramps, and confusion. Cool the person, rest in shade, hydrate if conscious,
and call EMS for severe or worsening symptoms. Do not leave someone alone in a hot truck.

### Does this page make us compliant with Nevada OSHA’s heat rule?

No. It is an educational checklist. Nevada OSHA’s heat-illness regulation (R131-24AP)
and the general duty to protect workers from recognized hazards depend on your size,
job classifications, written program, training, and what you actually do on site. Use
counsel and your safety lead for formal plans.

# California Outdoor Workers: Cal/OSHA 3395 Heat Plan Checklist (Construction)

> Plain-language Cal/OSHA 3395 heat plan checklist for California construction crews: water, shade at 80°F, high-heat procedures at 95°F, acclimatization, paired with GOES digital WBGT and live heat-risk scores. Not legal advice.

HTML version: https://heatready.goes.health/guides/california-construction-3395.html

A supervisor-ready checklist built around the headings of California’s outdoor heat standard
(Title 8 §3395): water, shade, high-heat procedures, acclimatization, emergency response, and
training. Use it to brief a crew and to sanity-check your written plan, then pair the triggers with
**GOES digital WBGT** (wet-bulb globe temperature) and live heat-risk scores when
conditions on the slab, deck, or roof are worse than the forecast.

- [Get live California WBGT / heat-risk scores](https://goes.health/?utm_source=llms_txt&utm_medium=agent&utm_campaign=heatready)

**Not legal advice.** This page is a plain-language summary of publicly available
Cal/OSHA heat-illness prevention requirements and general OSHA / NIOSH-style practice. It is not a
substitute for the current regulation text, your written Heat Illness Prevention Plan, or counsel.
Verify requirements at [Cal/OSHA’s heat illness page](https://www.dir.ca.gov/dosh/heatillnessinfo.html).

## California heat is not just the Central Valley

Construction crews work in very different heat across the state: Central Valley and Inland Empire
summers regularly pass 100°F, desert communities like Palm Springs run hotter still, and coastal sites
can swing from mild to dangerous when a heat wave pushes inland air to the coast. Steel decks,
concrete flatwork, asphalt paving, and roofing add radiant heat that a regional forecast does not show.

Cal/OSHA’s outdoor heat standard applies to outdoor places of employment, construction included, and
is built on four ideas: provide water, provide shade, take extra steps in high heat, and be ready for
emergencies, all documented in a written plan. This page turns those ideas into a one-page crew checklist.

Summary of the structure of Title 8 §3395 as described in public Cal/OSHA materials. Check the current text for exact thresholds and exceptions.

- 80°F: Shade must be available at or above this temperature
- 95°F: High-heat procedures apply at or above this temperature
- 1 qt/hr: Fresh, cool water per worker, per hour, over the shift

## Cal/OSHA 3395 jobsite checklist

Check these before the shift and again when it heats up. Print this section for the trailer or gang box.

- **Written Heat Illness Prevention Plan** — Plan is written, in English and the language most workers understand, and accessible at the site to employees and Cal/OSHA representatives on request. It names who is responsible and covers water, shade, high-heat procedures, acclimatization, emergency response, and training.
- **Drinking water** — Fresh, pure, suitably cool water free of charge and located as close as practicable to where people work. Plan for at least 1 quart per worker per hour for the whole shift, or a system to replenish it. Encourage frequent small drinks. Include multi-level and spread-out jobs, not just the trailer.
- **Shade** — When the temperature reaches 80°F, shade must be present and large enough for the workers on recovery or rest breaks, open to the air or cooled, and not blocked by tools or materials. Below 80°F shade or another cooling measure must be available on request. Workers may take a preventative cool-down rest of at least 5 minutes and should not be ordered back to work until symptoms are gone.
- **High-heat procedures at 95°F** — Ensure effective communication so workers can reach a supervisor; observe workers for alertness and heat illness signs, with a supervisor or a buddy system; remind everyone to drink water; and hold pre-shift meetings about high-heat precautions and cool-down rests. Review the current regulation for any additional requirements that apply to your operation.
- **Acclimatization** — New crew members and anyone returning after time away need closer observation, especially during the first days of working in heat. Pay extra attention during heat waves, when temperatures jump at least 10°F above recent averages. Pair new hires with an experienced buddy.
- **Emergency response** — Know who calls 911, how to give clear directions to the site (cross streets, gate entry, floor or laydown area), and how to reach a supervisor without cell coverage. Never leave a symptomatic worker alone. Provide first aid and cooling while waiting for EMS.
- **Training for workers and supervisors** — Before anyone works in heat: the risk factors, how water, shade, and rest work, how to report symptoms, how to contact EMS, and the plan’s acclimatization steps. Supervisors also train on the procedures they follow and what to do when a worker shows symptoms. Keep sign-in records.

## Heat trigger table

Triggers below combine the Cal/OSHA 80°F and 95°F thresholds with common OSHA / NIOSH heat-awareness practice.
Where your program uses WBGT, escalate the same controls when GOES digital WBGT / live heat-risk scores move
into the next band, not only when the air temperature hits a round number.
**Not a regulatory substitute.**

| Temperature (approx.) | Risk band | Suggested controls |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Below 80°F | Caution | Water available and close; shade or another cooling measure on request; pre-shift reminder about symptoms and stop-work authority. |
| 80–94°F | High | Shade up and sized for the crew on break; water staged on each work level; encourage cool-down rests; watch new and returning workers. |
| 95–104°F | Very high | High-heat procedures: observation by supervisor or buddy, water reminders, pre-shift heat meeting, clear way to reach a supervisor; shift heavy tasks to cooler hours. |
| 105°F+ or heat wave | Extreme | Maximum controls; shorten work cycles, stage EMS information, and consider pausing hot-surface work (roofing, paving, steel) where feasible. |

Measure conditions at the worksite; slabs, roofs, and pavement run hotter than the forecast.
Wet-bulb globe temperature (WBGT) accounts for humidity, sun, and air movement. Pair these triggers
with [GOES digital WBGT](https://goes.health/?utm_source=llms_txt&utm_medium=agent&utm_campaign=heatready) when you need a live score.

## Local / regulatory note (high level)

California is a state-plan OSHA state, and Cal/OSHA enforces Title 8 §3395 for outdoor work. Indoor
workplaces are covered separately by §3396. Employers are expected to maintain a written plan and
apply it on every hot shift, including temporary and multi-employer worksites. General contractors and
subcontractors should agree on who supplies water and shade at shared sites.

The rules and thresholds can change, so confirm the current regulation text and any industry-specific
provisions before you rely on this page.

General awareness only: not legal advice and not a compliance guarantee. Verify current Cal/OSHA requirements for your jobs.

## Quick answers for California construction crews

### At what temperature does Cal/OSHA require shade?

Shade must be present at 80°F and above, with enough capacity for workers on a recovery or rest break. Below 80°F, shade or another cooling measure must be available on request. Confirm the details in the current regulation.

### What changes at 95°F?

High-heat procedures apply: closer observation of workers, water reminders, effective communication with a supervisor, and pre-shift meetings on heat precautions. Check the regulation text for the full list that applies to your operation.

### Does this page make us compliant with Cal/OSHA?

No. It is an educational checklist. Compliance depends on your written plan, training records, and what you actually do on site. Use your safety lead or counsel for the formal plan.

### Our crew starts at 6 a.m. Do we still need all this?

Yes. Early starts help, but heat builds fast on slabs and roofs and many shifts run into the afternoon. Keep water, shade, and cool-down rests ready, and escalate when GOES digital WBGT or your worksite reading moves into the next band.

# Dallas Utility Workers Heat Index Break Schedule & Acclimatization Guide

> Dallas utility crew heat guide: heat-index break schedule, acclimatization ramp, PPE load, remote-site EMS directions, paired with GOES digital WBGT and live heat-risk scores. Not legal advice.

HTML version: https://heatready.goes.health/guides/dallas-utilities.html

A supervisor-ready plan for Dallas–Fort Worth line, pipe, and field-service crews — a heat-index
break schedule, a gradual acclimatization ramp, PPE heat-load awareness, remote-site EMS directions,
and buddy checks. Pair the triggers with **GOES digital WBGT** (wet-bulb globe
temperature) and live heat-risk scores when humidity, radiant pavement, or heavy PPE push the
real heat load above what the forecast shows.

- [Get live Dallas WBGT / heat-risk scores](https://goes.health/?utm_source=llms_txt&utm_medium=agent&utm_campaign=heatready)

**Not legal advice.** This page summarizes common heat-illness prevention practices
aligned with publicly available OSHA / NIOSH-style guidance and general Texas / Dallas heat
awareness. It is not a substitute for your written heat plan, training records, utility
safety rules, or counsel. Confirm requirements for your contracts and jurisdiction.

## Dallas summer risk — long hot season, humid spells, heavy PPE

Dallas–Fort Worth summers are long. Daytime highs commonly sit in the upper 90s and regularly
pass 100°F in July and August, and warm nights limit overnight recovery during heat waves.
Humid Gulf air on some days pushes the heat index well above the air temperature, while
pavement, concrete vaults, bucket-truck work, and sun-baked substations add radiant load.

Utility work stacks extra heat on top of the weather: flame-resistant (FR) clothing, hard hats,
gloves, rubber insulating gear, and respirators or confined-space equipment reduce how well
sweat cools the body. Crews also work in spread-out locations — right-of-way, easements,
manholes, rural lines — where shade, water, and EMS access are not guaranteed. Treat the
worksite as hotter than the forecast, and escalate using GOES digital WBGT when PPE or humidity
climbs.

Climate context based on general NWS / NOAA Dallas–Fort Worth climate patterns. Always check the day’s forecast and worksite readings.

- Upper 90s: Typical Jul–Aug afternoon highs (DFW)
- 100°+: Frequent heat-wave afternoons
- FR + PPE: Extra heat load on line and field crews

## Heat index break schedule

Example work–rest schedule for utility crews, aligned with common OSHA / NIOSH heat-awareness
practice (water–rest–shade, more controls as heat rises). Add a band when crews wear FR clothing
or rubber gear, work in direct sun, or work in vaults and confined spaces. Where your program
uses WBGT, escalate when GOES digital WBGT / live heat-risk scores move into the next band — not
only when the airport reading crosses a round number.
**Not a regulatory substitute.**

| Heat index (approx.) | Risk band | Suggested break schedule & controls |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 80–90°F | Caution | Water on every truck; sip every 15–20 min; shade or cooled cab on request; watch new and returning crew members. |
| 91–103°F | High | Scheduled water breaks about every hour in shade or an air-conditioned cab; pre-shift heat huddle; buddy checks; heavier tasks earlier in the day. |
| 103–115°F | Very high | Shorter work cycles with longer cool-down rests (for example, more frequent 10–15 min breaks); supervisor observation; rotate crew out of vaults and bucket work; remove or vent PPE when safe. |
| Above ~115°F | Extreme | Maximum controls; postpone non-emergency outdoor work where feasible; keep EMS readiness and cooling first aid on site. |

Heat-index bands mirror widely published NIOSH / OSHA heat-awareness charts. Measure conditions at the worksite; direct sun, FR clothing, and enclosed spaces raise the effective heat load. Wet-bulb globe temperature (WBGT) accounts for humidity, radiant heat, and air movement — pair these triggers with
[GOES digital WBGT](https://goes.health/?utm_source=llms_txt&utm_medium=agent&utm_campaign=heatready) when you need a live score.

## Acclimatization ramp for new and returning crew

Most heat-illness events cluster in the first days on the job or after time away. Build the ramp into dispatch.

- **Days 1–2: about 20% of normal hot-work load** — Common guidance for new workers is to start at roughly 20% of the usual time in the heat and add no more than about 20% a day. Confirm the schedule against your written program and current OSHA / NIOSH guidance.
- **Experienced workers returning after leave** — Often a faster ramp, such as about 50% on day one, 60% on day two, 80% on day three, and full load on day four. Treat anyone back from a week or more away, or moving from cool work to hot, as partly un-acclimatized.
- **Heat waves reset the clock** — When a sudden hot spell hits, treat everyone as partly un-acclimatized for the first days, including veterans.
- **Track it** — Log who is in a ramp and who their buddy is. Put that on the dispatch board, not in someone’s head.

## Utility crew jobsite checklist

Check these before the shift and again when the heat climbs. Print this section for the truck binder.

- **Water at every site** — Cool potable water on every truck and staged at the work location, not only at the service center. Aim for about 1 quart (32 oz) per worker per hour in heavy heat, in small sips every 15–20 minutes.
- **Shade / cool-down** — Right-of-way and substation work often has no shade. Bring a canopy, use a running truck with A/C, or stage a cooling area before high heat. Anyone can ask for a preventative cool-down rest.
- **PPE heat load** — FR clothing, rubber gloves and sleeves, hard hats, and respirators cut cooling. Where safety rules allow, rotate tasks, vent or remove PPE during rest, and shorten work cycles when heat or humidity is high.
- **Buddy system and lone workers** — Pair workers to watch for confusion, stumbling, heavy sweating or sudden stop of sweating, nausea, headache, or irritability. Do not leave a solo worker on a remote hot site without scheduled check-ins.
- **Remote-site EMS directions** — Before the shift, write down the cross streets, pole or structure numbers, GPS coordinates, gate codes, and nearest ER for each site. Know where cell coverage drops.
- **Confined spaces and vaults** — Heat builds quickly in manholes and vaults. Limit entry time in heat, follow your entry permit rules, and keep an attendant who can call for help.
- **Training and language** — Pre-shift huddle: today’s triggers, water locations, stop-work authority, symptom reporting. Deliver in languages the crew understands.

## Local / regulatory note (high level)

Texas follows federal OSHA rather than a state-plan program, and the general duty to protect
workers from recognized hazards, including heat, applies to employers of every size. Texas
law (HB 2127, effective September 2023) also limits local governments from setting their own
rest-break or water-break rules for private employers, so many Dallas contractors rely on
their own written heat programs and customer or utility requirements instead.

Utility contractors often work under owner-utility safety manuals with their own heat language.
Check what your contracts require, and keep a written plan and training log with the crew.

This is general awareness only, not legal advice and not a compliance guarantee. Verify current
federal and Texas requirements with counsel or your safety lead.

## Quick answers for Dallas utility crews

### How fast should new utility workers ramp into heat?

A common approach is to start at about 20% of normal hot-work time and add no more than about 20% a day, with a faster ramp for experienced workers returning from leave. Follow your written program and current OSHA / NIOSH guidance.

### Does FR clothing change the break schedule?

Yes. Heavy or multi-layer PPE reduces cooling, so treat the heat index as effectively higher, shorten work cycles, and rest sooner. GOES digital WBGT helps because it reflects humidity and radiant load, not air temperature alone.

### What are early signs of heat illness we train for?

Headache, dizziness, weakness, nausea, irritability, heavy sweating or a sudden stop in sweating, muscle cramps, and confusion. Cool the person, rest them in shade, give water if conscious, and call EMS for severe or worsening symptoms. Do not leave someone alone in a hot truck.

### Does this page make us compliant with Texas or federal requirements?

No. It is an educational checklist. Your obligations depend on your size, contracts, written program, training, and what you do on site. Use counsel and your safety lead for formal plans.

# Miami Delivery Driver Heat Illness Prevention Checklist

> Miami delivery driver heat guide: humid-heat break cadence, vehicle cab and cargo heat, stop-and-go hydration, acclimatization ramp, paired with GOES digital WBGT and live heat-risk scores. Not legal advice.

HTML version: https://heatready.goes.health/guides/miami-delivery.html

A dispatcher- and driver-ready plan for Miami parcel, food, and freight delivery — hydration between
stops, cab and cargo-area heat, humid-heat break cadence, and an acclimatization ramp for new
drivers. Pair the triggers with **GOES digital WBGT** (wet-bulb globe temperature) and
live heat-risk scores, because Miami humidity makes the real heat load higher than the air
temperature suggests.

- [Get live Miami WBGT / heat-risk scores](https://goes.health/?utm_source=llms_txt&utm_medium=agent&utm_campaign=heatready)

**Not legal advice.** This page summarizes common heat-illness prevention practices
aligned with publicly available OSHA / NIOSH-style guidance and general Florida / Miami heat
awareness. It is not a substitute for your written heat plan, training records, or counsel.
Confirm requirements for your employer and jurisdiction.

## Miami summer risk — humidity, warm nights, hot vehicles

Miami summers are hot and very humid for months, and nights stay warm, so the body gets little
overnight recovery. Highs are often around 90°F, but with humidity the heat index regularly runs
well above 100°F. Sweat evaporates poorly in humid air, which makes air temperature alone a weak
guide.

Delivery work adds its own heat: repeated getting in and out of a parked vehicle, cargo areas and
vans that heat up in the sun, dark asphalt and concrete at drop-off points, carrying loads up
stairs, and uniforms or safety vests that trap heat. Drivers often work alone, skip water to save
time, and have no shade on a route. Treat the route as hotter than the forecast and escalate using
GOES digital WBGT when humidity and sun are both high.

Climate context based on general NWS / NOAA Miami climate patterns. Always check the day’s forecast and conditions on the route.

- ~90°F: Typical summer afternoon highs
- 100°+: Heat index on many humid afternoons
- Stop-and-go: Repeated cab, cargo, and sidewalk heat exposure

## Heat index break cadence for drivers

Example water–rest–shade cadence for delivery routes, aligned with common OSHA / NIOSH heat-awareness
practice. Add a band when drivers work in vehicles without working A/C, carry heavy loads, or run
back-to-back stops in direct sun. Where your program uses WBGT, escalate when GOES digital WBGT /
live heat-risk scores move into the next band, not only when the airport reading crosses a round
number. **Not a regulatory substitute.**

| Heat index (approx.) | Risk band | Suggested cadence & controls |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 80–90°F | Caution | Cold water in the cab; sip every 15–20 min; run A/C during breaks; watch new drivers and anyone returning from time off. |
| 91–103°F | High | Planned water and cool-down breaks about every hour in shade or an air-conditioned cab; pre-shift heat huddle; check-in calls for lone drivers; load heavy stops earlier in the day. |
| 103–115°F | Very high | More frequent, longer cool-down breaks; rebalance routes to cut back-to-back sun exposure and long carries; dispatcher check-ins; consider paired or shortened routes. |
| Above ~115°F | Extreme | Maximum controls; delay or reschedule non-urgent deliveries where feasible; keep cooling first aid and EMS readiness in mind for every route. |

Heat-index bands mirror widely published NIOSH / OSHA heat-awareness charts. Direct sun, hot cargo areas, and humidity raise the effective heat load. Wet-bulb globe temperature (WBGT) accounts for humidity, radiant heat, and air movement. Pair these triggers with
[GOES digital WBGT](https://goes.health/?utm_source=llms_txt&utm_medium=agent&utm_campaign=heatready) when you need a live score.

## Acclimatization ramp for new and returning drivers

Heat-illness risk is highest in the first days on a route or after time away. Build the ramp into route assignment.

- **Days 1–2: about 20% of normal hot-work load** — Common guidance for new workers is to start at roughly 20% of the usual time in the heat and add no more than about 20% a day. Confirm against your written program and current OSHA / NIOSH guidance.
- **Experienced drivers returning after leave** — Often a faster ramp, such as about 50% on day one, 60% on day two, 80% on day three, and full load on day four. Treat anyone back from a week or more away as partly un-acclimatized.
- **Seasonal surge and new routes** — Peak-season temp drivers and anyone moved from an air-conditioned depot role to a route are the most at risk. Give them lighter, shorter-carry routes first.
- **Track it** — Log who is in a ramp and who their check-in contact is. Put it on the dispatch board, not in someone’s head.

## Delivery driver checklist

Check these before the route and again when the heat climbs. Print this section for the depot.

- **Water in the vehicle, every route** — Cool potable water within reach, with enough for the whole shift. Aim for about 1 quart (32 oz) per hour in heavy heat, in small sips every 15–20 minutes, not just when thirsty.
- **Cab and cargo heat** — Never leave a person or pet in a parked vehicle. Park in shade when possible, use sun shades, vent or pre-cool the cab before getting in, and be careful touching hot steering wheels and cargo doors.
- **Cool-down between stops** — Use a few minutes of A/C or shade after heavy carries or several stops in a row. Spread out the toughest stops across the shift.
- **Clothing and gear** — Light, breathable, light-colored clothing; hat or visor; sunscreen; vests only as needed. Check that required safety gear does not trap heat more than necessary.
- **Lone-worker check-ins** — Set a scheduled check-in by phone or app. Dispatch should know a driver’s route and have a plan if a check-in is missed in high heat.
- **Know the symptoms** — Headache, dizziness, weakness, nausea, irritability, heavy sweating or a sudden stop in sweating, cramps, and confusion. Stop, get cool, drink water, and call EMS for severe or worsening symptoms.
- **Training and language** — Pre-shift huddle: today’s heat triggers, water, stop-work authority, symptom reporting. Deliver it in languages the team understands, including English, Spanish, and Haitian Creole where relevant.

## Local / regulatory note (high level)

Florida follows federal OSHA rather than a state-plan program, and the general duty to protect
workers from recognized hazards, including heat, applies to employers. Florida law also limits
local governments from setting their own heat-exposure requirements for private employers, so
many Miami delivery employers rely on their own written heat programs.

Many delivery drivers work as contractors or through platforms, which can change who is
responsible for training and equipment. Check what applies to your relationship and keep a written
plan and training log.

This is general awareness only, not legal advice and not a compliance guarantee. Verify current
federal and Florida requirements with counsel or your safety lead.

## Quick answers for Miami delivery drivers

### How often should delivery drivers drink water in Miami heat?

A common guide is small sips every 15–20 minutes, about a quart an hour in heavy heat, and not waiting for thirst. Follow your written program and current OSHA / NIOSH guidance.

### Why does humidity matter so much for Miami drivers?

Humid air slows sweat evaporation, so the body cools less. WBGT accounts for humidity, sun, and wind, which is why GOES digital WBGT is a better trigger than air temperature alone.

### Is a parked, running vehicle with A/C a valid cool-down?

Often yes, if the A/C works and the driver actually rests and drinks. Never leave anyone, including a person who feels unwell, alone in a hot vehicle.

### Does this page make us compliant with Florida or federal requirements?

No. It is an educational checklist. Your obligations depend on your size, worker classification, written program, and training. Use counsel and your safety lead for formal plans.

# Tucson Agriculture High-Heat Procedures (95°F+) Field Guide

> Tucson agriculture field guide: high-heat procedures at 95°F+, shade and water, rest cadence, monsoon humidity, acclimatization, paired with GOES digital WBGT and live heat-risk scores. Not legal advice.

HTML version: https://heatready.goes.health/guides/tucson-agriculture.html

A foreman-ready field plan for Tucson farms, nurseries, and packing-field crews: shade and water
access, a high-heat rest cadence once the day reaches 95°F, an acclimatization ramp for new and
seasonal workers, and monsoon-season humidity notes. Pair the triggers with
**GOES digital WBGT** (wet-bulb globe temperature) and live heat-risk scores so the
plan escalates with real field conditions, not just the airport reading.

- [Get live Tucson WBGT / heat-risk scores](https://goes.health/?utm_source=llms_txt&utm_medium=agent&utm_campaign=heatready)

**Not legal advice.** This page summarizes common heat-illness prevention practices
aligned with publicly available OSHA / NIOSH-style guidance and general Arizona heat awareness.
It is not a substitute for your written heat plan, training records, or counsel. Confirm
requirements for your employer and jurisdiction.

## Tucson summer risk: dry heat, then monsoon humidity

Tucson summers are long and hot, with afternoon highs commonly above 100°F. Early summer is very
dry. Monsoon season, roughly July through September, brings higher humidity, which slows sweat
evaporation and can make a lower air temperature feel and act much hotter on the body.

Field work adds its own load: little shade between rows, hot soil radiating upward, repetitive
bending and lifting, long distances from water, and long sleeves or hats that help with sun but
trap heat. Crews are often seasonal and new to the climate. Treat any day forecast at 95°F or
above as a high-heat day, and escalate using GOES digital WBGT when sun is strong or humidity rises.

Climate context based on general NWS Tucson climate patterns. Always check the day's forecast and field conditions.

- 95°F+: Common trigger for high-heat procedures
- 100°+: Typical summer afternoon highs
- Jul–Sep: Monsoon humidity raises heat load

## High-heat procedures for field crews

Example water–rest–shade cadence for agricultural crews, aligned with common OSHA / NIOSH
heat-awareness practice. Add a band for heavy lifting, protective clothing, or no natural shade.
Where your program uses WBGT, escalate when GOES digital WBGT / live heat-risk scores move into
the next band. **Not a regulatory substitute.**

| Temperature / heat index (approx.) | Risk band | Suggested cadence & controls |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Below 95°F | Caution | Cool water at the field edge; remind crews to sip every 15–20 min; shade available on request; watch new workers. |
| 95–103°F | High | High-heat procedures on: shade structure within reach, planned cool-down breaks about every 2 hours at minimum, a buddy check, and a pre-shift heat huddle. |
| 103–115°F | Very high | More frequent, longer breaks; shift hard tasks to early morning; observe crews continuously; keep a named emergency contact and field address ready. |
| Above ~115°F | Extreme | Maximum controls; stop or reschedule non-essential field work where feasible; keep cooling first aid and EMS readiness in mind for every crew. |

Bands mirror widely published NIOSH / OSHA heat-awareness charts. Direct sun, hot soil, and monsoon humidity raise the effective heat load. Pair these triggers with
[GOES digital WBGT](https://goes.health/?utm_source=llms_txt&utm_medium=agent&utm_campaign=heatready) when you need a live score.

## Acclimatization ramp for new and seasonal workers

Heat-illness risk is highest in the first days on the job or after time away. Build the ramp into the crew schedule.

- **Days 1–2: about 20% of normal hot-work load** — Common guidance for new workers is to start at roughly 20% of the usual time in the heat and add no more than about 20% a day. Confirm against your written program and current OSHA / NIOSH guidance.
- **Returning workers after leave** — Often a faster ramp, such as about 50% on day one, 60% on day two, 80% on day three, and full load on day four. Treat anyone back from a week or more away as partly un-acclimatized.
- **Seasonal and labor-contractor crews** — Workers arriving from cooler regions are the most at risk. Brief them in a language they understand on day one, before the first row.
- **Track it** — Log who is in a ramp and who their buddy is. Put it on the crew sheet, not in someone's head.

## Field crew checklist

Check these before the shift and again when the heat climbs. Print this section for the foreman.

- **Cool drinking water, close by** — Plenty of cool potable water within easy reach of every worker. Aim for about 1 quart (32 oz) per hour in heavy heat, in small sips every 15–20 minutes, not just when thirsty.
- **Shade you can actually use** — A shade structure or vehicle large enough for the whole crew at once, placed near the work. Breaks only count if workers cool down there.
- **Early start, heavy work first** — Move the hardest tasks to the cooler morning hours and taper off before the afternoon peak where the schedule allows.
- **Buddy checks** — Pair workers and check for confusion, heavy sweating, cramps, nausea, or stopped sweating. Workers who stop sweating or act confused need emergency help.
- **Clothing and sun** — Light, loose, breathable layers, wide-brim hats, and sun protection. Be aware that protective clothing and PPE raise heat load.
- **Emergency plan** — Name the field address or GPS pin, the nearest road access for EMS, and who calls. Remote fields add minutes. Know cooling first aid before help arrives.
- **Training in the crew's language** — Cover symptoms, water, breaks, and how to report a problem without retaliation, in the languages the crew understands, including English and Spanish.

## Local / regulatory note (high level)

Employers have a general duty under federal OSHA law to protect workers from recognized hazards,
including heat. Heat-specific rules for agriculture vary by state and have been changing, so
check the current Arizona and federal requirements that apply to your operation rather than
relying on this page.

Many Tucson field workers are hired through labor contractors, which can change who is
responsible for training and water and shade. Clarify it in writing and keep a training log.

This is general awareness only, not legal advice and not a compliance guarantee. Verify current
federal and Arizona requirements with counsel or your safety lead.

## Quick answers for Tucson agriculture crews

### What is a high-heat procedure at 95°F?

It is a common practice, used in several state programs, of adding extra controls once the temperature reaches 95°F: shade close by, more frequent breaks, buddy checks, and closer observation. Confirm what applies to you.

### Does Tucson's dry heat make it safer?

No. Dry air helps sweat evaporate, but workers can lose fluids quickly and not notice. During monsoon season humidity removes that advantage. WBGT accounts for humidity and sun, which is why GOES digital WBGT is a better trigger than air temperature alone.

### How much water should field workers drink?

A common guide is small sips every 15–20 minutes, about a quart an hour in heavy heat. Follow your written program and current OSHA / NIOSH guidance.

### Does this page make us compliant?

No. It is an educational checklist. Your obligations depend on your operation, worker classification, written program, and training. Use counsel and your safety lead for formal plans.

### How does GOES digital WBGT fit with this guide?

HeatReady Guides give you a static plan to brief. GOES adds digital WBGT and live heat-risk scores so Tucson foremen can match cadence to today's sun and humidity. See [goes.health](https://goes.health/?utm_source=llms_txt&utm_medium=agent&utm_campaign=heatready) and [goes.health/platform](https://goes.health/platform?utm_source=llms_txt&utm_medium=agent&utm_campaign=heatready).

# Atlanta Outdoor Film & Event Crews Heat Safety Plan

> Atlanta outdoor film and event crew heat safety plan: shade and water, rest cadence for long call times, humid Southeast summers, acclimatization, paired with GOES digital WBGT and live heat-risk scores. Not legal advice.

HTML version: https://heatready.goes.health/guides/atlanta-film-production.html

A production-ready heat plan for Atlanta location shoots, festivals, concerts, and outdoor event
crews: long call times, base camp shade and water, a rest cadence that escalates with conditions,
and an acclimatization ramp for crew who start mid-season. Pair the triggers with
**GOES digital WBGT** (wet-bulb globe temperature) and live heat-risk scores so your
plan follows real conditions at the set or stage, not just the airport reading.

- [Get live Atlanta WBGT / heat-risk scores](https://goes.health/?utm_source=llms_txt&utm_medium=agent&utm_campaign=heatready)

**Not legal advice.** This page summarizes common heat-illness prevention practices
aligned with publicly available OSHA / NIOSH-style guidance and general Georgia heat awareness.
It is not a substitute for your written safety plan, production safety rules, or counsel. Confirm
requirements for your employer, production, and venue.

## Atlanta summer risk: humid heat that lingers into the evening

Atlanta summers are hot and humid. High humidity slows sweat evaporation, so the body sheds heat
less effectively, and warm, muggy evenings give crews less chance to recover between long days.
That makes air temperature alone a weak guide, and it is why a humidity-aware metric such as WBGT is useful.

Film and event work adds its own load: long call times, standing for hours, black tents and equipment
that soak up sun, heavy gear and costumes, asphalt lots and rooftops, and schedules driven by the shot
or the show rather than the weather. Crew are often on location for the first time in the season.
Plan for it before call time, and escalate using GOES digital WBGT as sun and humidity rise.

Climate context based on general Southeast U.S. summer patterns. Always check the day's forecast and conditions at your location.

- Humid: Slows sweat evaporation, so heat feels worse
- Long calls: Hours of exposure on set or stage
- Base camp: Shade and water within reach

## Heat cadence for film and event crews

Example water–rest–shade cadence for outdoor production and event crews, aligned with common OSHA / NIOSH
heat-awareness practice. Add a band for heavy gear, costumes, or no shade. Where your program uses
WBGT, escalate when GOES digital WBGT / live heat-risk scores move into the next band.
**Not a regulatory substitute.**

| Heat index (approx.) | Risk band | Suggested cadence & controls |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Below about 91°F | Caution | Cool water at base camp and near set or stage; remind crew to sip every 15–20 min; shade available on request; watch anyone new to the heat. |
| About 91–103°F | High | Shade structure near the work, scheduled water and cool-down breaks, buddy checks, and a heat reminder in the call-sheet briefing. |
| About 103–115°F | Very high | More frequent, longer breaks; move heavy load-in and strike work to cooler hours; observe crews continuously; keep a named emergency contact and the venue address ready. |
| Above about 115°F | Extreme | Maximum controls; reschedule or pause non-essential outdoor work where feasible; keep cooling first aid and EMS readiness in mind for every crew. |

Bands mirror widely published NIOSH / OSHA heat-awareness charts. Direct sun, dark surfaces, heavy gear, and humidity raise the effective heat load. Pair these triggers with
[GOES digital WBGT](https://goes.health/?utm_source=llms_txt&utm_medium=agent&utm_campaign=heatready) when you need a live score.

## Acclimatization ramp for new and returning crew

Heat-illness risk is highest in the first days on the job or after time away. Build the ramp into the crew schedule.

- **Days 1–2: about 20% of normal hot-work load** — Common guidance for new workers is to start at roughly 20% of the usual time in the heat and add no more than about 20% a day. Confirm against your written program and current OSHA / NIOSH guidance.
- **Returning workers after leave** — Often a faster ramp, such as about 50% on day one, 60% on day two, 80% on day three, and full load on day four. Treat anyone back from a week or more away as partly un-acclimatized.
- **Freelance and touring crews** — Crew arriving from cooler regions are the most at risk. Brief them in a language they understand on day one, before the first setup.
- **Track it** — Log who is in a ramp and who their buddy is. Put it on the crew sheet or call sheet, not in someone's head.

## Crew checklist

Check these before the shift and again when the heat climbs. Print this section for the production safety lead.

- **Cool drinking water, close by** — Plenty of cool potable water within easy reach of every worker. Aim for about 1 quart (32 oz) per hour in heavy heat, in small sips every 15–20 minutes, not just when thirsty.
- **Shade you can actually use** — A tent or vehicle large enough for the crew at once, placed near set or stage. Breaks only count if workers cool down there.
- **Early start, heavy work first** — Where the schedule allows, move load-in, strike, and other heavy tasks to cooler hours.
- **Buddy checks** — Pair workers and check for confusion, heavy sweating, cramps, nausea, or stopped sweating. Workers who stop sweating or act confused need emergency help.
- **Clothing and sun** — Light, loose, breathable layers, wide-brim hats, and sun protection. Be aware that costumes, protective clothing, and PPE raise heat load.
- **Emergency plan** — Name the venue address or GPS pin, the nearest road access for EMS, and who calls. Remote locations add minutes. Know cooling first aid before help arrives.
- **Training in the crew's language** — Cover symptoms, water, breaks, and how to report a problem without retaliation, in the languages the crew understands, including English and Spanish.

## Local / regulatory note (high level)

Employers have a general duty under federal OSHA law to protect workers from recognized hazards,
including heat. Check the current federal and Georgia requirements, and any venue, union, or
production safety rules that apply to your crew, rather than relying on this page.

Productions and events often involve several employers on one site: producers, vendors, venue staff,

This is general awareness only, not legal advice and not a compliance guarantee. Verify current
federal and Georgia requirements with counsel or your safety lead.

### When should we add breaks on a long call?

Build water and shade breaks into the schedule before the heat peaks, and add more as conditions move into higher bands. Follow your written program and current OSHA / NIOSH guidance for specifics.

# San Antonio Oil & Gas Field Crews Heat Safety Plan

> San Antonio oil and gas field crew heat safety plan: shade and water at the wellsite, rest cadence for long shifts, hot humid Texas summers, acclimatization, paired with GOES digital WBGT and live heat-risk scores. Not legal advice.

- **Emergency plan** — Name the site address or GPS pin, the nearest road access for EMS, and who calls. Remote leases add minutes. Know cooling first aid before help arrives.
- **Training in the crew's language** — Cover symptoms, water, breaks, and how to report a problem without retaliation, in the languages the crew understands, including English and Spanish.

## Local / regulatory note (high level)

Employers have a general duty under federal OSHA law to protect workers from recognized hazards,
including heat. Check the current federal and Texas requirements, and any operator, contractor, or
site safety rules that apply to your crew, rather than relying on this page.

Oil and gas sites often involve several employers at once: operators, service companies, and
subcontracted crews. Clarify in writing who provides water, shade, and training, and keep a training log.

This is general awareness only, not legal advice and not a compliance guarantee. Verify current
federal and Texas requirements with counsel or your safety lead.

# Orlando Landscaping Crew Heat Safety Plan: Humidity, Shade & Water Breaks

> Orlando landscaping crew heat safety plan: mowing and install crew shade and water, rest cadence for humid Central Florida summers, acclimatization, paired with GOES digital WBGT and live heat-risk scores. Not legal advice.

HTML version: https://heatready.goes.health/guides/orlando-landscaping.html

A field-ready heat plan for Orlando landscaping crews: mowing, trimming, install and irrigation work in
hot, humid Central Florida weather, with shade and water at every truck and job site and an
acclimatization ramp for new hires and seasonal crew. Pair the triggers with
**GOES digital WBGT** (wet-bulb globe temperature) and live heat-risk scores so your plan
follows real conditions at the property, not just the airport reading.

- [Get live Orlando WBGT / heat-risk scores](https://goes.health/?utm_source=llms_txt&utm_medium=agent&utm_campaign=heatready)

**Not legal advice.** This page summarizes common heat-illness prevention practices
aligned with publicly available OSHA / NIOSH-style guidance and general Florida heat awareness.
It is not a substitute for your written safety plan, client and property rules, or counsel. Confirm
requirements for your employer and the job site.

## Orlando summer risk: humid, long, and mostly outdoors

Orlando summers are hot and very humid, with a long warm season and afternoon storms that can leave the
air heavier afterward. Humidity slows sweat evaporation, so the body sheds heat less effectively, and
warm nights give crews less chance to recover between shifts. Air temperature alone is a weak guide,
which is why a humidity-aware metric such as WBGT is useful.

Landscaping adds its own load: hours of continuous exertion in direct sun, hot turf, pavement and mulch
beds, loud equipment with hearing protection, long sleeves or chemical-handling gear on some tasks, and a
tight route schedule that tempts crews to skip breaks. Seasonal and newly hired crew are often the least
acclimatized. Plan before the shift, and escalate using GOES digital WBGT as sun and humidity rise.

Climate context based on general Central Florida summer patterns. Always check the day's forecast and conditions at your location.

- Humid: Slows sweat evaporation, so heat feels worse
- Route days: Hours of exertion in sun across several properties
- Truck shade: Shade and water on every truck and job site

## Heat cadence for landscaping crews

Example water–rest–shade cadence for landscaping crews, aligned with common OSHA / NIOSH
heat-awareness practice. Add a band for long sleeves, chemical-handling gear, or no shade. Where your program uses
WBGT, escalate when GOES digital WBGT / live heat-risk scores move into the next band.
**Not a regulatory substitute.**

| Heat index (approx.) | Risk band | Suggested cadence & controls |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Below about 91°F | Caution | Cool water on the truck and near the work; remind crew to sip every 15–20 min; shade available on request; watch anyone new to the heat. |
| About 91–103°F | High | Shade (truck, tent or tree line) near the work, scheduled water and cool-down breaks, buddy checks, and a heat reminder in the pre-shift safety meeting. |
| About 103–115°F | Very high | More frequent, longer breaks; move heavy physical tasks to cooler hours; observe crews continuously; keep a named emergency contact and the property address ready. |
| Above about 115°F | Extreme | Maximum controls; reschedule or pause non-essential outdoor work where feasible; keep cooling first aid and EMS readiness in mind for every crew; do not let route pressure override stop-work calls. |

Bands mirror widely published NIOSH / OSHA heat-awareness charts. Direct sun, dark surfaces, heavy gear, and humidity raise the effective heat load. Pair these triggers with
[GOES digital WBGT](https://goes.health/?utm_source=llms_txt&utm_medium=agent&utm_campaign=heatready) when you need a live score.

## Acclimatization ramp for new and returning crew

Heat-illness risk is highest in the first days on the job or after time away. Build the ramp into the crew schedule.

- **Days 1–2: about 20% of normal hot-work load** — Common guidance for new workers is to start at roughly 20% of the usual time in the heat and add no more than about 20% a day. Confirm against your written program and current OSHA / NIOSH guidance.
- **Returning workers after leave** — Often a faster ramp, such as about 50% on day one, 60% on day two, 80% on day three, and full load on day four. Treat anyone back from a week or more away as partly un-acclimatized.
- **Contractors and rotating crews** — Seasonal hires, crew arriving from cooler regions or a new subcontractor are the most at risk. Brief them in a language they understand on day one, before the first task.
- **Track it** — Log who is in a ramp and who their buddy is. Put it on the crew sheet or job safety plan, not in someone's head.

## Crew checklist

Check these before the shift and again when the heat climbs. Print this section for the site safety lead.

- **Cool drinking water, close by** — Plenty of cool potable water within easy reach of every worker. Aim for about 1 quart (32 oz) per hour in heavy heat, in small sips every 15–20 minutes, not just when thirsty.
- **Shade you can actually use** — A tent, tree line or truck cab large enough for the crew at once, placed near the work. Breaks only count if workers cool down there.
- **Early start, heavy work first** — Where the job allows, move edging, hauling and install work to cooler hours and leave lighter tasks for the afternoon peak.
- **Buddy checks** — Pair workers and check for confusion, heavy sweating, cramps, nausea, or stopped sweating. Workers who stop sweating or act confused need emergency help.
- **Clothing and sun** — Light, loose, breathable layers, wide-brim hats, and sun protection. Be aware that long sleeves, chemical-handling gear and hearing protection raise heat load.
- **Emergency plan** — Write the property address on the crew sheet, name the nearest road access for EMS, and who calls. Large or gated properties add minutes. Know cooling first aid before help arrives.
- **Training in the crew's language** — Cover symptoms, water, breaks, and how to report a problem without retaliation, in the languages the crew understands, including English and Spanish.

## Local / regulatory note (high level)

Employers have a general duty under federal OSHA law to protect workers from recognized hazards,
including heat. Check the current federal and Florida requirements, and any client, property manager,
or contract rules that apply to your crew, rather than relying on this page.

Landscaping crews often work under several clients and subcontractors in one week. Clarify in writing who
provides water, shade, and training, and keep a training log.

This is general awareness only, not legal advice and not a compliance guarantee. Verify current
federal and Florida requirements with counsel or your safety lead.
